title: AWS CEO Hiring 11K People While Everyone Panics About AI Jobs
metaDescription: AWS CEO just announced 11,000 new hires for 2026. While others worry about AI taking jobs, smart people are using this shift to get ahead.
author: Marty @ CertFlo

sections.heading: Amazon Just Showed Everyone What's Actually Happening
sections.body: While everyone's freaking out about AI stealing jobs, AWS CEO Matt Garman just said they're hiring 11,000 interns in 2026. Says demand for software jobs is "accelerating," not dying. Pretty much the opposite of what you keep hearing. According to Business Insider, other tech people are warning about AI messing with coding jobs. But here's what they're missing: AI isn't replacing people. It's creating work that didn't exist five years ago. The people who figured this out early aren't running from AI. They're running toward it.

sections.heading: Why This Actually Matters for You
sections.body:
Amazon's hiring thing tells you exactly where this is all going. Companies aren't cutting people who know AI — they're hunting for them. Every business needs someone who can connect regular work with AI stuff.

Most people around you are still treating AI like it's some weird curiosity or gonna kill their job. Meanwhile the people learning AI tools right now are setting themselves up as the person who can solve problems others just can't.

Think about it: when your company needs someone who can automate workflows, handle data at scale, or build AI solutions that save thousands of hours — who gets promoted? The person who learned this early or the one still doing everything by hand?

sections.heading: The Window's Closing
sections.body: Amazon's announcement means the companies that win are gonna be the ones who figure out how to mix human thinking with AI capabilities. They need people who can think strategically about automation and solve complex stuff that AI alone can't handle. Right now you have something rare. Most people are still sitting on the sidelines, which means learning AI automation now puts you in a pretty small group. You become the person others come to when they need AI problems solved. But this won't last forever. Once more people catch on, the advantage shrinks. The people learning AI skills right now — while it still feels early — those are the ones running departments in three years. If you're serious about getting ahead, having a structured plan helps you build these skills systematically and show leadership what you can do. Pretty simple choice: start building your AI skills now while you can still get ahead, or watch others pull away cause they mastered the tools reshaping everything.
